title: Shared infrastructure tests the boundary of India’s financial regulation
summary: Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu argued that rapid digital adoption gives the RBI earlier sight of some risks while shortening the time in which it can respond. Automated payments, lending and market activity operate continuously. An operational failure, fraud or shift in confidence can spread before conventional monitoring captures the deterioration. Digital finance has also improved access, productivity, competition and transparency. The regulatory problem is to preserve those gains while assigning responsibility for outcomes across a chain of regulated firms, unregulated providers and overseas infrastructure. The address sets out the deputy governor’s approach and examples of existing RBI work. It specifies no change in the policy rate, capital requirement or implementation deadline (paras. 2–5).

The trade-off between speed and predictability applies to the regulator itself. Frequent amendments can wear down compliance capacity and leave businesses uncertain about the rules governing investment. Slow changes can leave new exposures outside effective oversight. Prescriptive requirements are clear but can become obsolete; broad principles can produce uneven results when governance or enforcement is weak. Murmu favoured an adaptable approach supported by capable management, continuing supervisory engagement and enforcement. For a bank investor, an implication is that a firm’s advantage under flexible rules depends partly on whether it can demonstrate compliance in practice. The speech gives no estimate of compliance costs or how they are distributed between firms (paras. 4–5, 9).

Individual authorities can make sound decisions within their mandates while collectively missing a significant exposure. A non-financial platform can distribute services on behalf of several financial firms, with different regulators seeing different parts of the chain. Indian supervision combines activity-based requirements, exemplified by directions on credit and debit cards, with institution-based prudential rules. Oversight of conglomerates, directions for non-financial holding companies and the Financial Stability and Development Council’s inter-regulatory arrangements supplement these measures. The EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act and Singapore’s expert advisory panel are examples of different international responses. Differences across countries still leave scope for regulatory arbitrage and for discrepancies in the treatment of a common provider (paras. 6–8 and accompanying references).

One system-wide concern is a critical service with few substitutes. Strong capital positions across individual institutions can coexist with a shared dependence that interrupts their operations simultaneously. Opaque arrangements and unclear accountability can compound the disruption, while distorted information circulating online can change customer behaviour before facts are established. Models add another layer: bias or drift may become apparent only when a tool reaches scale. Murmu referred to India’s responsible AI committee report as a starting point requiring translation into regulation. In his account, institutions remain answerable for outcomes produced by models they use. Data protection, fraud controls and timely public communication are complementary because they address different points in this transmission chain (paras. 10–14).

Richer information also makes earlier intervention possible. The speaker cited the RBI’s machine-learning tool for identifying mule accounts, high-frequency information on transactions and the prospect of tracing common dependencies across institutions. Such analysis could reveal where an initial operational event might create subsequent liquidity pressure. Feedback from incidents, near misses and supervisory experience could help calibrate rules to the materiality of the risk. The address describes the intended use of these tools; it supplies no comparison of alerts with realised losses and no estimates of false positives. Faster reporting is a benefit only to the extent that supervisors can interpret signals and act on them (paras. 15–18).

The RBI has already placed regulatory services on its PRAVAAH portal. DAKSH supports supervisory workflows and incident reporting. The Advanced Supervisory Analytics Group uses digital techniques for microdata, governance and other assessments, while complaint-management tools can identify service and conduct problems. Murmu linked those systems to impact assessment, periodic reviews and stakeholder consultation. Digital information could reduce duplication as well as tighten oversight. His closing principles leave firms flexibility over the technologies they use, while expecting continuity of critical functions, orderly recovery and clear responsibility. The open investment question is how much of the efficiency gain remains after paying for governance, operational redundancy and scarce expertise. Neither net savings nor the impact on lending margins is established in the address (paras. 19–26, footnotes 13–16).

questions.question: Where would one provider’s failure simultaneously impair multiple regulated institutions?
questions.detail: Murmu identifies concentration and poor substitutability as systemic risks, but does not identify critical providers or give recovery times. The issue affects the diversification of exposures across financial issuers. Start with the RBI guidance on operational risk cited in footnote 11, then compare institutional disclosures on outsourcing, backup arrangements and test results. Look for the same provider appearing behind ostensibly independent alternatives.

questions.question: Do high-frequency indicators materially improve intervention decisions?
questions.detail: The RBI has deployed tools and outlined a role for transaction data and incident reports. The speech leaves open how often signals are actionable and how much time they save. This matters to estimates of both compliance spending and loss avoidance. Seek aggregate evaluation results for the cited tools, including false-positive rates, remediation times and comparable outcomes before adoption, alongside the annual-report sections referenced by the speaker.

questions.question: How much regulatory discretion can a digitally expanding bank exercise in practice?
questions.detail: The address favours proportionality and accountability, but the cost of demonstrating outcomes under principles-based rules remains uncertain. That cost could influence product economics and the relative attractiveness of in-house or outsourced systems. Compare the RBI’s regulatory impact assessments and consultation responses with institutions’ public disclosures on compliance investment and new-product economics. Check whether differences reflect scale or exposure as well as regulatory treatment.
